cells.tense: Right now imagination runs clean in you, and it runs through what you feel.
cells.ask: Pick one uncertain thing you've been circling, sit with how it actually feels for ten minutes before bed, and write down what shape it took.
cells.core:
You can feel how something is going to go before there's any evidence for it, and you don't argue with that feeling. When a situation is unclear, you don't freeze and you don't force it — you stay open to it the way you would to a person you just met, and something in you starts to see how it could go. That isn't naivety. It's imagination doing its work, and it arrives through feeling rather than argument.

The reason this holds is that you're not just sitting in the uncertainty. A steadier part of you keeps warm whatever this touches, so what you picture has somewhere to land. Feed that part now — move in a direction you actually feel like moving, not one you invented to seem busy.
cells.sheetLine: You can feel how something will go before it has happened.
cells.verb: meeting what isn't worked out yet with fresh feeling and seeing how it could go

cells.tense: You're already living in how this will land, and none of it has happened yet.
cells.ask: Name one thing you're carrying for someone who hasn't asked you to. Put it down for today.
cells.core:
You're ahead of it. Before anything has actually happened, you've felt out every version of how it might go, and you're already reacting to the one you're most afraid of. The picturing isn't the problem — what it's doing now is rehearsing futures nobody asked for, and you're spending real energy on scenes that haven't arrived.

Underneath, this is care that won't sit still. You tend things before they're handed to you, and that care has turned into gripping. What's being asked is smaller than it sounds: one thing you're carrying, set down. Not forever — for a day. Let what's right here in front of you steer you; the bracing is steering you now, and it's wearing you out.

cells.tense: You made a call about your own imagination a while back, and you're still standing in it.
cells.ask: Pick one vague thing that keeps nagging you and ask it one plain question — what is this actually made of? — then write whatever comes.
cells.core:
What this looks like going well is small and ordinary. You meet something unclear, you don't know yet, and that's fine — you poke at it, ask what it's made of, and let the answer be whatever it is. The not-knowing stays light instead of heavy, and the world keeps being interesting. That's the shape of it when it's working.

Right now it runs the other way: staying with what's right in front of you has become the whole of it, and unclear things read as weight rather than invitation. What's starved isn't imagination. It's the plain attention that feeds it. So don't try to feel more or dream bigger. Get curious about one small thing, ask what it's really made of, and let the answer be enough without being clever. Being alright with not knowing yet is the muscle that turns the lights back on.
cells.sheetLine: The curiosity went quiet, not the imagination.

cells.tense: You are already picturing how other people's days will go while you call it just being sensible.
cells.ask: Catch one such moment today and say, out loud or on paper: 'I pictured that.'
cells.core:
You do this and you don't call it anything. You walk into a room and you know the temperature of it. You hear a plan and you see the snag before anyone names it. You read how someone's week is about to go without checking with them first. None of that is guesswork — it's imagination running, and it runs so smoothly that you don't sign your name to it.

Seeing the bare shape of things is real work, and that's what makes it invisible: you see the shape and skip straight past the picturing of it. So the ask is only to notice once. Not to announce it to anyone or make it a policy — just catch one and own that you were the one picturing. What you do with it stays exactly as useful; only the name on it changes.
cells.sheetLine: You do this all the time. Call it yours once.

attempts.check: Unsupported claim: that this person is imaginative-with-others in the way the card describes — the record gives the capacity and its seat, not their history or motives. The reader could reasonably say 'I don't feel imaginative at all, I just handle what's in front of me,' which is exactly the disowned case and still workable. The asks all survive a wrong read: they are actions a camera could see and they teach something whether or not the map is right. The sentence that serves the writer more than them would be any line about 'trusting the mystery' or 'wide-eyed wonder' — cut; nobody needs to be told their own beginner's eyes.
